question: On 6 June 2025, the Commission published a feasibility study on how to address the trafficking of illegally sourced wildlife. This was discussed on 23 September 2025 in Parliament’s Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety (ENVI), where the Commission mentioned that resource constraints meant it would look at next steps only after the CITES Conference of the Parties (CoP).

Parliament’s resolution of 23 October 2025 on CITES1 urged the Commission to expand existing regulations and tools, including the trade control and expert system (TRACES), and to use the results of the feasibility study to present, as a priority, relevant legislative proposals to criminalise the trade and possession of illegally sourced wildlife.
The ‘Stolen Wildlife’ reports reveal the scale of the illegal trade in protected species and the role of the EU as both a hub and destination. 1.

As the CITES CoP has concluded, what is the first assessment of the feasibility study and what timeline is foreseen for proposing legislative proposals on data collection and criminalisation in relation to illegally sourced wildlife?

Will the Commission dedicate additional resources to the ENVI team responsible for this dossier, and to the team at the its Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety responsible for alignment with the TRACES database, so that a serious effort can be undertaken to tackle illegally sourced wildlife?

Resolution of 23 October 2025 on the EU strategic objectives for the 20th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), to be held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from 24 November to 5 December 2025 (2025/2618(RSP)), texts adopted, P10_TA(2025)0255.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.3.2026) The Commission is currently analysing the findings of the exploratory feasibility study1, together with the views expressed by stakeholders. The study does not prejudge any future legislative or non-legislative measures, and no decisions have been taken at this stage on proposals concerning data collection or criminalisation related to illegally sourced wildlife.

The Commission will examine the issues raised as part of its ongoing analysis, including in relation to data collection. Any future work would need to be consistent with ongoing efforts on electronic permitting and ensure coherence with related customs systems. The Commission remains committed to continued dialogue with all relevant stakeholders throughout this process.
